summary: HELIOS is a 3D health digital twin designed to support astronauts during space missions. It integrates nine body systems into an interactive model that allows astronauts to monitor 16 health indicators, report symptoms, and receive personalized medical guidance. It addresses the challenge of limited medical support during long-distance missions by comparing health data with NASA standards or each astronaut’s personal baseline. It also provides step-by-step protocols adapted to communication delays, works offline, and records medical events for flight surgeons. This project is important because, as missions travel farther from Earth, astronauts must become more independent in managing their health. HELIOS helps detect potential health problems early, supports safer decisions, and connects medical care with available onboard resources. Its approach could also benefit people in remote areas on Earth with limited access to medical services.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

HELIOS is a 3D health twin for astronauts. Each of nine body systems, built from the BodyParts3D anatomical atlas, is a data object whose live status (nominal, caution or critical) sets its color on an interactive body. The twin opens as an astronaut in a suit; “Explore my body” scans through the suit and reveals the anatomy system by system.

Astronauts log 16 health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, sleep, mood, glucose, cabin CO₂, retinal thickness, radiation dose and more), tap the 3D body to report discomfort, and dictate notes by voice, all offline. HELIOS judges each value against a NASA limit where one exists (cabin CO₂, NASA-STD-3001; retinal thickness, NASA SANS criteria). Everywhere else, it compares the value with the astronaut’s own baseline from their first 14 days, using three calibrated statistical rules.

Every alert follows detect, treat, verify: it shows where its threshold comes from, lists protocol steps by authority level, and closes only when the indicator is measured back in range. A triage answers “What should I do now?” and adapts to distance from Earth. On the station, the advice is to contact the flight surgeon. On Mars, where a reply takes about 44 minutes, it is to start the onboard protocol. “Send to Flight Surgeon” plays that real delay, and if the link is lost, the report is queued and sent automatically when the signal returns. Each episode becomes an exportable SOAP note. HELIOS also reads real space weather (NOAA GOES, NASA DONKI) and checks whether a protocol can be carried out with the supplies and trained crew on board.

2. What benefits does it have?

One visual place for health data, readable without medical training: the body shows what needs attention, and guidance is in plain language.

Personal, with few false alarms: where NASA sets no limit, each astronaut is compared with themselves. The detectors are calibrated to about a 4% chance of a false caution per indicator over 30 days.

Trustworthy: every alert shows its source and the kind of evidence behind it, and illustrative ranges are never presented as NASA limits.

It confirms that a treatment worked: an action counts as successful only when the measurement returns to range, not when it has been carried out.

Safe by default: medication steps are withheld unless the mission medical plan pre-authorizes them.

It keeps working when Earth can’t help: offline operation, store-and-forward when the signal is lost, and advice that accounts for the communication delay.

It connects health with logistics: inventory, expiry dates and crew training show whether a protocol can actually be done, and supplies can be found by scanning their QR label.

Every episode is documented as a SOAP note and timeline, ready for the flight surgeons.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

As missions go farther from Earth, medical support has to move on board. NASA calls this Earth-Independent Medical Operations (EIMO): the gradual transfer of medical decisions from ground teams to the crew. A round trip to the station takes seconds, but to Mars it can take up to about 44 minutes, and there are periods when Earth cannot be reached at all.

HELIOS is a concept for that future: decision support for the crew, not a prescription. It helps astronauts notice changes early against their own normal, act first with approved onboard protocols, and hand the flight surgeons a complete record when the link returns. The same approach could also serve people far from medical care on Earth, such as polar stations, ships or remote communities. Its three parts are monitoring against your own baseline, showing the evidence behind every alert, and working offline.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Languages: TypeScript for the app logic, rules engine and statistics; JavaScript with Node.js for the local API server and data scripts; SQL (SQLite); HTML and CSS.

3D and interface: Three.js with three-mesh-bvh for fast picking on the anatomical model, GSAP for camera moves and transitions, and Vite for development and builds. The anatomy comes from the BodyParts3D atlas (CC BY 4.0), reduced with glTF-Transform and meshoptimizer.

Voice: Vosk (vosk-browser) with a bundled English model, so speech recognition runs in the browser and no audio leaves the device.

Storage: IndexedDB in the browser for the medical inventory, and SQLite (node:sqlite) for the local API’s alerts, interventions and verifications.

Browser APIs: the microphone for dictation, and the camera with BarcodeDetector to scan QR labels on medical supplies (labels generated with qrcode-generator).

Testing: Vitest for the rules engine, statistics, simulator and API.

Data: NOAA SWPC (GOES proton flux), NASA DONKI (solar particle events), NASA NTRS and the Human Research Program (evidence and risks), NASA OSDR, and PhysioNet’s MMASH dataset, used to validate the detectors with real heart-rate and sleep data.

Collaboration: Git and GitHub with pull requests.

AI: the source code was written with the assistance of Claude Code (Anthropic). The idea and design decisions are the team’s.

5. How is your project creative?

HELIOS treats the body as a data structure: every system is an object, and its health sets its color on the 3D body. The body is also an input: astronauts tap where it hurts, and the pin stays on the body and in their history.

The advice changes with distance from Earth. The same finding says “contact the flight surgeon” on the station and “start the onboard protocol” on Mars. “Send to Flight Surgeon” makes the delay visible as a signal traveling to a small Earth. When the link is lost, reports wait on board and leave on their own when the signal returns.

It is honest by design: only two thresholds are NASA limits, and the app says so. Everything else compares each astronaut with their own normal, and every alert carries its evidence.

It also builds a routine and tells a story. A daily check-in shows what changed since yesterday and the plan for the day, and every episode is kept as a SOAP record. “Play the Mission” is a 90-second guided episode that shows detection, guidance, a consultation from the station and from Mars, treatment and verification.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Communication: delays grow with distance and the link can drop, so HELIOS works offline, queues reports for the next contact, and adapts its advice to the delay.

Users: not every astronaut is a doctor, and their hands are often busy. The interface uses plain language, voice dictation and step-by-step guidance, and every line says where it comes from (measured, reported, protocol, triage).

Safety and scope: HELIOS supports decisions; it does not diagnose. A discomfort report never changes a status, medication steps need pre-authorization in the medical plan, and every protocol step shows its authority level.

Scientific validity: for most indicators NASA sets no limit, so we use each astronaut’s own baseline. We calibrated the detectors for few false alarms, validated them with real data, and state the trade-off: small, slow changes take days to flag.

Environments: the station, a lunar base, Mars transit and the Mars surface change the radiation dose rate, gravity and signal delay. Space weather comes from real NOAA and NASA data.

Resources: with no resupply, a protocol is only useful if the supplies and trained crew exist, so the app checks inventory, expiry dates and training.

Accessibility and privacy: status uses symbols as well as color, motion can be reduced, charts work with the keyboard, and voice and health data stay on the device.
